note: First follow-up bite on PR 180's findings. NFC normalization at the top of StringMatcher.normalize so composed and decomposed forms of the same visible word collide — surfaced fresh in the pr213/pr180 review pass as the wall a --seed policy-vi or --seed policy-ar would hit. Companion decision to 0199 (walk-through). Does NOT address the two other PR 180 findings (adversarial homoglyphs, pure-emoji collapse) — those need their own decisions.

decisions.question: Should StringMatcher.normalize NFC-fold its input before the legacy pipeline (lowercase + strip non-word + collapse whitespace)?
decisions.commitment: Yes. `nestor/matcher.py:191-206` calls `unicodedata.normalize('NFC', text)` before the existing regex pipeline. NFC is idempotent (the Matcher Protocol requires normalize(normalize(x)) == normalize(x); NFC and the legacy pipeline are individually idempotent, so the composition is). For 7-bit ASCII the NFC step is a no-op and downstream is unchanged — every sealed row that existed before this change normalizes to the exact same key it normalized to before, asserted in tests/test_matcher_nfc.py::test_ascii_normalizes_byte_for_byte_as_before. Gated by 9 tests in tests/test_matcher_nfc.py (composed/decomposed collision for Vietnamese ư, café, and Arabic diacritic; idempotence over the full sample; four must-preserve tests for Cyrillic ≠ Latin, fullwidth ≠ ASCII, pure-emoji → empty, ASCII byte-for-byte; and one end-to-end integration through memory.add_pair / best_sealed). All 177 tests in tests/test_unconventional.py (PR 180) still pass, so the three invariants PR 180 locked (homoglyph distinctness, fullwidth distinctness, emoji-collapses-to-empty) are preserved.
decisions.why: PR 180 filed 'homoglyph blindness' as one adversarial finding (Cyrillic а surviving normalize as distinct from Latin a). The review-branch pass surfaced a companion case with the opposite framing: characters like Vietnamese ư (U+01B0), Icelandic ð, IPA ɣ are the ORDINARY vocabulary of their languages, not attacks. At the codepoint level normalize handles them fine — the bug is when the same visible letter comes in as a precomposed codepoint on one side and as a base letter + combining mark on the other (which is what happens between keyboard input and PDF paste, and what most Vietnamese and Arabic source text looks like in the wild). Before this change, `Người` typed with U+01B0 normalized differently from `Người` typed as u + U+031B, because `re.sub(r'[^\w\s]')` strips the combining horn silently. That would bite hand-off item 5's `--seed policy-vi` / `policy-ar` on real seeded content, without any test firing until an operator reported a missing seal. NFC fixes it without touching the adversarial-homoglyph question (NFC does not fold Cyrillic а into Latin a — that is a confusable-mapping question, not a composition question) and without touching the emoji-collapse question (emoji are non-\w regardless of composition). The two remaining PR 180 findings each need their own decision-and-bench cycle.

decisions.question: Why NFC rather than NFKC (which additionally folds fullwidth digits, superscripts, ligatures, etc.)?
decisions.commitment: NFC only. NFKC would fold `１２３` (fullwidth) into `123` (ASCII), fi ligature into f+i, superscript ² into 2, etc. PR 180's test_fullwidth_vs_ascii_digits locks that fullwidth stays distinct — that would break under NFKC. NFC is the canonical composition form and touches ONLY composition equivalence (visually-identical rendering, same intended letter, different Unicode bytes); NFKC folds compatibility equivalence (visually-similar rendering, arguably-same intent, definitely different content). This PR fixes the composition question and leaves compatibility folding as a separate future decision the operator can consider if they see concrete need.
decisions.why: The bar for changing normalize is 'the operator sees a letter on their screen, and the store treats it the same way the operator does.' NFC clears that bar (composed and decomposed forms render identically because they're the same abstract letter). NFKC clears a wider bar but at the cost of collapsing distinctions that carry meaning: fullwidth digits are the digits used in Japanese phone numbers and are distinguished on purpose from ASCII; superscripts are formulas; ligatures may or may not be intended by the source. A future PR that wants NFKC folding needs to measure what real corpora rely on the distinction and either scope the fold per-domain or decide the trade-off explicitly. This PR does not.
